# The finite-base obstruction already has homothetic simplex fibers

This is a second exact counterexample to the UNRESTRICTED finite-base
gamma_d/h(P) target. Like the earlier rectangle example, it is NOT an
OC counterexample: the measured bases are not a complete lattice
intersection. Here every continuous fiber is a homothetic copy of one
simplex about the same vertex, and its scale is a positive increasing
concave function on the projection.

Let T={(x,y):x>=0,y>=0,x+y<=1}, let t=1/100, and put

    P={0,t,1},
    K_0=(5/19)T, K_t=T, K_1=(39/38)T.                (1)

Let C be the convex hull of these three fibers. Its sections are
exactly r(z)T, where r is the piecewise affine function interpolating
the three displayed radii. Indeed the first slope is
(1-5/19)/t=1400/19, while the second is
(39/38-1)/(1-t)=50/1881; both are positive and the first is larger.
Thus r is concave, its hypograph is the convex hull of the three
vertical radius segments, and the indicated fibers are actual sections.
Equivalently the only nontrivial anchored inclusion is strict:

    (1-t)K_0+tK_1=(1029/3800)T subset K_t.            (2)

The areas and their sum are

    a=25/722, b=1/2, c=1521/2888,
    M=3065/2888.

Put Q=169/722=676/2888.

## Exact finite cap cover

At the middle base use

    H_0={-x-y-2(z-t)>=-12/19},
    H_1={ x  -2(z-t)>= 6/19},
    H_2={ y  -2(z-t)>= 6/19}.                       (3)

Their margins sum to zero on z=t, so they cover that entire plane.
At z=0, H_0 contains K_0 and the other two miss it, since

    5/19 < 6/19-1/50,
    5/19 < 12/19+1/50.

At z=1 all three caps miss K_1: the first's threshold for -x-y is
-12/19+99/50>0, and each other's threshold is
6/19+99/50>39/38. On K_t their areas are respectively144/722,
169/722,169/722. Consequently all three mixed cap masses are Q,
because144/722+25/722=169/722.

At the first base use the three isolating caps

    {-x-y-100z>=-10/57},
    { x  -100z>=  5/57},
    { y  -100z>=  5/57}.                            (4)

They cover its whole plane, exclude both other fibers, and each
captures area(10/57)^2/2=50/3249<Q from K_0. At z=t the largest
left sides are -1,0,0 respectively, already strictly below the
thresholds. At z=1 the exclusions are stronger.

At the last base use

    {-x-y+2(z-1)>=-13/19},
    { x  +2(z-1)>= 13/38},
    { y  +2(z-1)>= 13/38}.                          (5)

They cover its whole plane and strictly exclude the first two fibers.
At z=t their maximum left sides are -99/50,1-99/50,1-99/50;
the values at z=0 are smaller than the corresponding thresholds too.
On K_1 all three areas equal(13/19)^2/2=Q.

The nine caps (3)-(5) cover every candidate plane with individual
mass at most Q. Thus the finite union's maximum depth is at most Q/M.
Its last-fiber centroid (1,13/38,13/38) has depth at least
gamma_2 c/M=Q/M from that fiber alone, by ordinary Grünbaum. Every
closed ambient halfspace is included in this lower bound; a whole-fiber
restriction contributes even more. Therefore the exact maximum is

    max_depth=676/3065 < 2/9=gamma_2/h(P),            (6)
    2/9-676/3065=46/27585>0.

Here h(P)=2, since convex traces on three ordered collinear points
are interval traces. The same first-and-last trace argument used in
the earlier counterexample gives both inequalities for h(P).

The continuous triangles have common orientation and vertex, and their
volume roots are proportional to the positive concave increasing r.
Thus those properties do not repair the false arbitrary-sampling
claim. Replacing the base by{0,1,100} and taking ALL integer fibers
would introduce the positive fibers at2,...,99, whose contributions
cannot be omitted. The result does not contradict a theorem that uses
consecutive integer samples, including the archived equal-spacing
simplex-chain theorems.
